cells: Polluter must bear cost of environmental damage.
Prevent harm even if scientific certainty is lacking.

blocks.content: Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation.

rows: Anticipate and prevent harm before it occurs, shifting burden of proof to the developer.
Polluter pays costs of pollution control, ecological restoration, and victim compensation.

items: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) explicitly incorporated the 'Precautionary Principle' and 'Polluter Pays Principle' into Indian environmental jurisprudence.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) established the doctrine of 'Absolute Liability' for hazardous industries, removing exceptions available under strict liability.
Differentiate Article 48A (Directive Principle instructing the State to protect forests and wildlife) from Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty of citizens to protect the natural environment).

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Precautionary Principle dictates that lack of full scientific certainty shall not postpone cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation.
The Polluter Pays Principle shifts the financial burden of pollution remediation and compensation onto the polluter.
The Public Trust Doctrine mandates that certain natural resources are held by the government in trust for the free and unimpeded use of the general public.
The Indian Judiciary integrated international environmental principles into domestic law primarily under Article 21 (Right to Life) of the Constitution.
